lessons.title: ухо (úkho) — "ear," and Russian's third gender finally arrives
lessons.gloss: ear — neuter, the first word Russian gives its third gender, and a word-for-word cousin of the English ear

segments.text: A new chapter, a new part of the body, and the last of Chapter 6's three genders — held back until now, on purpose.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — ухо

segments.text: ухо — úkho — ear. Neuter.
Stress on the first syllable: Ú-kho. Ends in -о, so — finally — Chapter 6's third row: -о and -е mark the neuter, and here is the first word in this book to actually wear it.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a straight inheritance, no detour

segments.text: ухо (úkho) is Indo-European h₂ous-, and the cousin web is about as tight as this book gets: English ear is the same word; so is Latin auris ( becomes auricle, aural), and Greek ous ( becomes otitis, an ear infection). Four languages, one unbroken thread from a single ancient root — no borrowing, no replacement, nothing lost along the way.

That makes ухо (úkho) the plainest kind of cousin in this book: not a loanword like kófe, not a word that replaced an older one, just the same PIE root worn down four different ways in four different mouths.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ухо" — stress on the front, neuter]
[YOU SAY: the third row — "-о and -е, neuter"]

segments.instruction: "ear, auris, ous" — one root, three languages
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ear, auris, ous" — one root, three languages]

segments.text: Say "ear." (Úkho.) What gender is it, and which ending finally shows it? (Neuter — -о.) Name two other languages that share the same root word for "ear." (English ear, Latin auris — also Greek ous.) Is this word borrowed or inherited? (Inherited, straight from PIE, no detour.)

lessons.title: нос — "nose," a second straight cousin in a row
lessons.gloss: nose — masculine, and the same word as English nose and Latin nasus

segments.text: One syllable, one gender back to consonant-final masculine, and another word that never left the family.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — нос

segments.text: нос — nos — nose. Masculine.
Consonant-final, back to the first row of Chapter 6's table. Every letter is one you have read since Chapter 1.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the plainest cousin yet

segments.text: нос is Indo-European nas-, and it barely needs translating: English nose is the same word, and so is Latin nasus ( becomes nasal, nasturtium, the "nose-twisting" flower). Say nos next to nose and nasus and the family resemblance needs no explaining at all.
Two body-part words in a row, úkho and нос (nos), and both are the same kind of cousin: no loan, no replacement, just the same ancient root, worn down along three different paths to the same meaning.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair so far — "úkho, нос"]

segments.text: Say "nose," with its gender. (Нос — masculine.) Name its two closest cousins. (English nose, Latin nasus.) What English flower name comes from the Latin cousin? (Nasturtium.) Which earlier word in this chapter is the same kind of straight inheritance? (Úkho, "ear.")

lessons.title: рот (rot) — "mouth," where the cousin trail actually runs out
lessons.gloss: mouth — masculine, and this time the resemblance to English is not there to trust

segments.text: Two straight cousins in a row was good luck, not the rule. This one has no secure English relative at all — and it belongs to a verb you already own.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — рот

segments.text: рот — rot — mouth. Masculine.
Consonant-final, masculine again. (On paper this romanizes exactly like the English word rot — another spelling coincidence, like Russian drug and English drug, with no shared history at all.)

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — an honest dead end, and the mouth that speaks

segments.text: Úkho and нос (nos) both handed you a clean English cousin. рот does not. Its Proto-Slavic ancestor rŭtŭ originally meant "beak, snout" and is probably related to ryt', "to dig, to burrow" — the picture of an animal's snout rooting through the ground, later widened to any mouth, including yours. There is no secure link to English mouth at all: English's word comes from an entirely separate Germanic root, munþaz, with no shared ancestor here. Where Chapter 4's chitát had no English descendant, this word has no English ancestor in common — a different kind of dead end, and worth naming exactly that plainly rather than forcing a connection that isn't there.

What рот (rot) does have is a job you have been practising since Chapter 3: it is what makes govorít' possible. You met г as Greek gamma on govorít''s very first line; here is the mouth that has been saying it ever since.

segments.instruction: "рот (rot), govorít'" — the mouth, and what it has been doing since Chapter 3

segments.text: Say "mouth," with its gender. (Рот — masculine.) Is it related to English mouth? (No — separate Germanic root, no shared ancestor.) What is its own best guess of an origin? (Ryt', "to dig" — a snout rooting the ground.) Which Chapter 3 verb does the mouth make possible, and what letter did that verb first teach you? (Govorít'; the letter г, Greek gamma.)

lessons.title: глаз (glaz) — "eye," the word for the eye that isn't the word for the eye
lessons.gloss: eye — masculine, and the word that quietly evicted Russian's inherited word for eye

segments.text: The last of four face words, and the strangest story in the chapter: Russian's everyday word for "eye" is not the word Indo-European gave it for "eye" at all.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — глаз

segments.text: глаз — glaz — eye. Masculine.
Consonant-final, masculine, closing the chapter's four with the same pattern that opened it in Chapter 6.

(Tempting, on the page, to link this to English glass — the spellings even rhyme. Resist it: they trace to two different PIE roots and are not cousins. Its real story is stranger than that coincidence.)

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a slang word that won

segments.text: Every other body word in this chapter kept its ancient Indo-European name. Glaz did not. Glaz began in Old Russian as glazŭ, "a ball, a glass bead, a smooth round stone" — PIE g(ʰ)el-, "round." Starting around the sixteenth century it spread as slang for "eyeball," then simply "eye," and it completely displaced the true inherited word.

That older word was oko (plural ochi) — PIE h₃ókʷs, the actual, secure cousin of English eye itself, the same root behind Latin oculus ( becomes ocular, monocle) and Greek ophthalmós. Oko still exists, but only in poetry and set phrases now. Its one everyday survivor is hiding in plain sight: ochki, "eyeglasses," is built directly on ochi — literally "little eyes." So the word that means eye in Russian today is a Slavic upstart; the word that is actually your cousin only shows up when you put spectacles on.
This is Chapter 3's vídet' completed at last: the organ that does the seeing turns out to have replaced its own name, while the verb for seeing stayed put the whole time.

segments.text: Say "eye," with its gender. (Glaz — masculine.) What did глаз (glaz) originally mean, and what word did it push out? ("Round object, ball"; it displaced oko.) Where does the true inherited eye-word survive today? (Ochki, "glasses" — literally "little eyes.") Name all four face words this chapter taught, in order. (Úkho, нос (nos), рот (rot), глаз (glaz).) Which Chapter 3 verb does the eye make possible, and what sound-swap did that verb teach in its I form? (Vídet'; д becomes zh, as in vízhu.)
